questions.stem: What are the products of the electrolysis of molten lead bromide (PbBr₂)?

options.text: Lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Lead at the anode and bromine at the cathode
Lead oxide at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
Bromine at the cathode and lead at the anode

questions.explanation: Lead ions (Pb²⁺) are positive, so they move to the cathode (negative electrode) where they gain electrons to form lead metal. Bromide ions (Br⁻) are negative, so they move to the anode (positive electrode) where they lose electrons to form bromine.

questions.stem: What is the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode during electrolysis of molten sodium chloride?

options.text: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻

questions.explanation: At the cathode, sodium ions gain electrons (are reduced): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. This produces sodium metal. The cathode is where reduction always occurs during electrolysis.

questions.stem: Why is electrolysis used to extract aluminium rather than reduction with carbon?

options.text: Because aluminium does not form an oxide
Because aluminium is cheaper to extract by electrolysis
Because aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide
Because carbon would make aluminium impure

questions.explanation: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series. Carbon is not reactive enough to displace aluminium from its oxide. Therefore, the more expensive process of electrolysis must be used to extract aluminium.

questions.stem: In the extraction of aluminium, why is cryolite added to the aluminium oxide?

options.text: To remove impurities from the aluminium
To lower the melting point of aluminium oxide, reducing energy costs
To act as the reducing agent
To make the aluminium stronger

questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000°C). Adding cryolite lowers the melting point of the mixture to about 950°C, which significantly reduces the energy needed and therefore the cost of extraction.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide, what forms at the anode?

options.text: Aluminium metal
Oxygen gas
Water
Hydrogen gas

questions.explanation: Oxide ions (O²⁻) are attracted to the positive anode where they lose electrons and form oxygen gas: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. The aluminium forms at the cathode.

questions.stem: Why do the carbon anodes need to be replaced regularly during the extraction of aluminium?

options.text: Because they become too hot
Because they dissolve in the cryolite
Because the oxygen produced at the anode reacts with the carbon electrodes, burning them away
Because aluminium deposits on them

questions.explanation: The oxygen gas produced at the anode reacts with the hot carbon electrodes to form carbon dioxide: C + O₂ → CO₂. This gradually burns away the anodes, so they must be replaced regularly.

questions.stem: When predicting the products of electrolysis of a molten binary ionic compound, where does the metal form?

options.text: At both electrodes equally
At the cathode, because metal ions are positive and attracted to the negative electrode
At the anode, because metal ions are positive
In the electrolyte solution

questions.explanation: Metal ions are positive (cations). They are attracted to the cathode (negative electrode) where they gain electrons and are deposited as the pure metal. The non-metal forms at the anode.
